questions.question: Q1. State Newton's law of cooling.
questions.answer: The rate of loss of heat of a body is proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings: −dQ/dt = hS(T − T_s) (constant h, S, T_s).
questions.example: Tea cools fast when hot, slowly when near room T.

questions.question: Q2. Define specific heat capacity. State its SI unit.
questions.answer: Specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by 1 °C: c = Q/(mΔT). SI unit = J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.example: Water c ≈ 4180 J/kg·K (high, why it's a good coolant).

questions.question: Q3. Explain the method of mixtures to find specific heat of a solid.
questions.answer: Heat the solid to a known temperature, drop it into a known mass of cooler water in an insulated calorimeter. Heat lost = heat gained: m_s c_s(T_s−T_f) = [m_w c_w + C_cal](T_f−T_w). Solve for c_s.
questions.shortcut: heat lost = heat gained; solve for the unknown c.
questions.example: A hot metal chip cools the water; equate the energies.

questions.question: Q4. Why does water have a high specific heat? State a practical consequence.
questions.answer: Water has a high specific heat (≈4180 J/kg·K), so it can absorb/release large heat with little temperature change. It is used as a coolant in engines and for coast-moderating ocean water temperatures.
questions.shortcut: High c → big heat with small ΔT; coolant use.
questions.example: An engine radiator uses water's high c.

questions.question: Q5. Find the heat needed to raise 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C.
questions.answer: Q = mcΔT = 2×4180×60 = 501 600 J ≈ 5.02×10⁵ J. ▥ 11.1 Newton's Law of Cooling & 11.2 Specific Heat  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Newton's Law of Cooling vs Specific Heat Specific Heat: c at constant P vs c at constant V ▣ 11.3–11.5 Latent Heat & Triple Point

questions.question: Q6. Define latent heat and specific latent heat.
questions.answer: Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a change of state at constant temperature. Specific latent heat is that per unit mass: L = Q/m, in J/kg. It is large because it breaks/reforms intermolecular bonds.
questions.shortcut: L = Q/m ; no ΔT during phase change.
questions.example: Water at 100 °C absorbs 2.26×10⁶ J/kg to become steam.

questions.question: Q7. Find the heat to convert 100 g of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C. L_f = 3.34×10⁵ J/kg.
questions.example: ≈ 33 kJ of latent heat of fusion.

questions.question: Q8. Differentiate latent heat of fusion and vaporization.
questions.answer: Latent heat of fusion (L_f) is for solid ⇄ liquid; latent heat of vaporization (L_v) is for liquid ⇄ gas. L_v is much larger because vaporization requires overcoming intermolecular forces to go to a gas (large volume increase).

questions.question: Q9. Define the triple point of a substance.
questions.answer: The triple point is the unique combination of temperature and pressure at which the solid, liquid and gas phases coexist in equilibrium. It is a fixed calibration point; for water it is 0.01 °C and 611 Pa.
questions.example: The 273.16 K fixed point of the Kelvin scale (historically).

questions.question: Q10. Explain why dry ice (solid CO₂) sublimates at normal pressure.
questions.answer: At 1 atm the CO₂ triple point (−56.6 °C, 5.1 atm) is above 1 atm, so solid CO₂ cannot exist as a liquid at 1 atm; it changes directly to gas (sublimation). ▥ 11.3–11.5 Latent Heat & Triple Point  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Latent Heat of Fusion vs Vaporisation Triple Point vs Critical Point PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: 1 atm < triple-point pressure → sublimation, no liquid.
questions.example: Dry ice vanishes without liquid, giving fog.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the method of mixtures for the specific heat of a solid.
theoryItems.answer: Heat the solid to T_s, put it into m_w water at T_w in a calorimeter of heat capacity C_cal. Heat lost = heat gained: m_s c_s(T_s−T_f) = [m_w c_w + C_cal](T_f − T_w). Solve for c_s.

theoryItems.question: [State] T2. Define specific heat capacity, specific latent heat and the units.
theoryItems.answer: Specific heat c = Q/(mΔT) (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) — heat to raise unit mass by 1 K. Specific latent heat L = Q/m (J kg⁻¹) — heat for unit mass to change state at constant T.
theoryItems.shortcut: c: per °C per mass; L: per mass, no ΔT.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T3. Compare the specific heats of metals and non-metals.
theoryItems.answer: Metals have low specific heats (high thermal conductivity, few degrees of freedom per atom for heat); non-metals like water and wood have high specific heats (more energy to raise temperature). This is why metals heat up quickly and water resists temperature change.
theoryItems.shortcut: Metals: low c; water/insulators: high c.
theoryItems.example: A metal spoon heats fast; a cup of water heats slowly.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T4. Explain Newton's law of cooling and its logarithmic plot.
theoryItems.answer: The rate of heat loss is proportional to the excess temperature: −dQ/dt = hS(T − T_s). Integrating gives T − T_s = (T₀ − T_s)e^{−kt}, so ln(T − T_s) is linear in time with negative slope; the body cools faster when hotter.
theoryItems.example: A hot cup cools quickly at first, slowly later.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain latent heat of fusion and vaporization, and why L_v > L_f.
theoryItems.answer: Fusion (solid⇄liquid) and vaporization (liquid⇄gas) occur at constant temperature with heat going into breaking intermolecular bonds. L_v is much larger because vaporization requires overcoming all cohesive forces and a large volume increase, far more than melting.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain the method of the ice calorimeter to find L_f.
theoryItems.answer: Weigh known hot water (or a hot body) and add it to a known mass of ice at 0 °C in an insulated container; the melted-ice mass gives the heat absorbed. L_f = [heat given up by hot water] / [mass of ice melted] (correcting for water cooling).
theoryItems.example: Measures the latent heat of fusion of ice.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the triple point and its role in the temperature scale.
theoryItems.answer: The triple point is the unique (T, P) where solid, liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium. For water it is 0.01 °C and 611 Pa, and it was historically used as the fixed 273.16 K reference for the thermodynamic scale.
theoryItems.example: It defines a reproducible calibration point.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T8. Why does the temperature of a substance stay constant during a change of state?
theoryItems.answer: The added heat goes into doing work against intermolecular forces (latent heat), changing the arrangement of particles, rather than increasing their kinetic energy; since temperature measures kinetic energy, it stays constant until the change is complete.
theoryItems.shortcut: All heat → latent (breaks bonds), not KE → T constant.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T9. Find the total heat to convert 100 g of ice at −10 °C to water at 30 °C. (c_ice=2000, c_w=4180, L_f=3.34×10⁵ J/kg).
theoryItems.shortcut: Sum: warm ice + melt + warm water.

▣ 11.1 Newton's Law of Cooling & 11.2 Specific Heat
Q1. State Newton's law of cooling.
Answer:  The rate of loss of heat of a body is proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings: −dQ/dt = hS(T − T_s) (constant h, S, T_s).
⚡ Shortcut:  Rate ∝ (T − T_s); hotter → cools faster.
Example:  Tea cools fast when hot, slowly when near room T.
Q2. Define specific heat capacity. State its SI unit.
Answer:  Specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by 1 °C: c = Q/(mΔT). SI unit = J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
⚡ Shortcut:  c = Q/(mΔT).
Example:  Water c ≈ 4180 J/kg·K (high, why it's a good coolant).
Q3. Explain the method of mixtures to find specific heat of a solid.

Answer:  Heat the solid to a known temperature, drop it into a known mass of cooler water in an insulated calorimeter. Heat lost = heat gained: m_s c_s(T_s−T_f) = [m_w c_w + C_cal](T_f−T_w). Solve for c_s.
⚡ Shortcut:  heat lost = heat gained; solve for the unknown c.
Example:  A hot metal chip cools the water; equate the energies.
Q4. Why does water have a high specific heat? State a practical consequence.

Answer:  Water has a high specific heat (≈4180 J/kg·K), so it can absorb/release large heat with little temperature change. It is used as a coolant in engines and for coast-moderating ocean water temperatures.
⚡ Shortcut:  High c → big heat with small ΔT; coolant use.
Example:  An engine radiator uses water's high c.
Q5. Find the heat needed to raise 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C.
⚡ Shortcut:  Q = mcΔT.
Example:  ≈ 0.5 MJ.

▣ 11.3–11.5 Latent Heat & Triple Point
Q6. Define latent heat and specific latent heat.

Answer:  Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a change of state at constant temperature. Specific latent heat is that per unit mass: L = Q/m, in J/kg. It is large because it breaks/reforms intermolecular bonds.
⚡ Shortcut:  L = Q/m ; no ΔT during phase change.
Example:  Water at 100 °C absorbs 2.26×10⁶ J/kg to become steam.
Q7. Find the heat to convert 100 g of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C. L_f = 3.34×10⁵ J/kg.
⚡ Shortcut:  Q = mL_f at 0 °C.
Example:  ≈ 33 kJ of latent heat of fusion.
Q8. Differentiate latent heat of fusion and vaporization.

Answer:  Latent heat of fusion (L_f) is for solid ⇄ liquid; latent heat of vaporization (L_v) is for liquid ⇄ gas. L_v is much larger because vaporization requires overcoming intermolecular forces to go to a gas (large volume increase).
⚡ Shortcut:  L_v > L_f (vaporization overcomes more forces).
Example:  Water: L_f≈3.3×10⁵, L_v≈2.26×10⁶ J/kg.
Q9. Define the triple point of a substance.

Answer:  The triple point is the unique combination of temperature and pressure at which the solid, liquid and gas phases coexist in equilibrium. It is a fixed calibration point; for water it is 0.01 °C and 611 Pa.
⚡ Shortcut:  S+L+G coexist; water: 0.01 °C, 611 Pa.
Example:  The 273.16 K fixed point of the Kelvin scale (historically).
Q10. Explain why dry ice (solid CO₂) sublimates at normal pressure.
Answer:  At 1 atm the CO₂ triple point (−56.6 °C, 5.1 atm) is above 1 atm, so solid CO₂ cannot exist as a liquid at 1 atm; it changes directly to gas (sublimation).
⚡ Shortcut:  1 atm < triple-point pressure → sublimation, no liquid.
Example:  Dry ice vanishes without liquid, giving fog.

▹ Derive  (derivations & long answers)
[Derive] T1. Derive the method of mixtures for the specific heat of a solid.
Answer:  Heat the solid to T_s, put it into m_w water at T_w in a calorimeter of heat capacity C_cal. Heat lost = heat gained: m_s c_s(T_s−T_f) = [m_w c_w + C_cal](T_f − T_w). Solve for c_s.
⚡ Short / exam line:  c_s = [m_w c_w + C_cal](T_f−T_w) / [m_s(T_s−T_f)].
Example:  Assumes an insulated vessel (no loss).
▹ State  (definitions, laws & formulae)
[State] T2. Define specific heat capacity, specific latent heat and the units.
Answer:  Specific heat c = Q/(mΔT) (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) — heat to raise unit mass by 1 K. Specific latent heat L = Q/m (J kg⁻¹) — heat for unit mass to change state at constant T.
⚡ Short / exam line:  c: per °C per mass; L: per mass, no ΔT.
Example:  Water c≈4180; L_f(ice)≈3.3×10⁵; L_v(water)≈2.26×10⁶ J/kg.
▹ Compare  (compare & contrast)
[Compare] T3. Compare the specific heats of metals and non-metals.

Answer:  Metals have low specific heats (high thermal conductivity, few degrees of freedom per atom for heat); non-metals like water and wood have high specific heats (more energy to raise temperature). This is why metals heat up quickly and water resists temperature change.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Metals: low c; water/insulators: high c.
Example:  A metal spoon heats fast; a cup of water heats slowly.
▹ Explain  (working / principle / application)
[Explain] T4. Explain Newton's law of cooling and its logarithmic plot.

Answer:  The rate of heat loss is proportional to the excess temperature: −dQ/dt = hS(T − T_s). Integrating gives T − T_s = (T₀ − T_s)e^{−kt}, so ln(T − T_s) is linear in time with negative slope; the body cools faster when hotter.
⚡ Short / exam line:  ln(T−T_s) vs t = straight line.
Example:  A hot cup cools quickly at first, slowly later.
[Explain] T5. Explain latent heat of fusion and vaporization, and why L_v > L_f.

Answer:  Fusion (solid⇄liquid) and vaporization (liquid⇄gas) occur at constant temperature with heat going into breaking intermolecular bonds. L_v is much larger because vaporization requires overcoming all cohesive forces and a large volume increase, far more than melting.
⚡ Short / exam line:  L_v ≫ L_f (vaporization breaks more bonds).
Example:  Water: L_v≈2.26×10⁶ vs L_f≈3.3×10⁵ J/kg.
[Explain] T6. Explain the method of the ice calorimeter to find L_f.

Answer:  Weigh known hot water (or a hot body) and add it to a known mass of ice at 0 °C in an insulated container; the melted-ice mass gives the heat absorbed. L_f = [heat given up by hot water] / [mass of ice melted] (correcting for water cooling).
⚡ Short / exam line:  L_f = heat supplied / ice melted.
Example:  Measures the latent heat of fusion of ice.
[Explain] T7. Explain the triple point and its role in the temperature scale.

Answer:  The triple point is the unique (T, P) where solid, liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium. For water it is 0.01 °C and 611 Pa, and it was historically used as the fixed 273.16 K reference for the thermodynamic scale.
⚡ Short / exam line:  S+L+G coexist; water: 0.01 °C, 611 Pa.
Example:  It defines a reproducible calibration point.
▹ Why  (conceptual & 'why' questions)
[Why] T8. Why does the temperature of a substance stay constant during a change of state?

Answer:  The added heat goes into doing work against intermolecular forces (latent heat), changing the arrangement of particles, rather than increasing their kinetic energy; since temperature measures kinetic energy, it stays constant until the change is complete.
⚡ Short / exam line:  All heat → latent (breaks bonds), not KE → T constant.
Example:  Ice stays at 0 °C while melting.

⚡ Short / exam line:  Sum: warm ice + melt + warm water.
